claims.claim: Last-move compression: if H is k-uniform and its classical Maker-Breaker duration τ(H)=t is finite, then θ(H)≤max{k,t−1}. More precisely, θ(H)=k when t=k, while θ(H)≤t−1 when t>k.
claims.evidence: A classical win needs at least k Maker moves and any token-game win needs k simultaneous Maker tokens, so t≥k and θ(H)≥k. Fix a classical strategy S winning within t Maker moves. During the first t−1 token moves, Maker uses fresh tokens and maintains a legal virtual classical play: virtual Maker claims equal her actual tokens, while the monotone virtual Breaker set contains the actual blue set. After an actual Breaker response, add its destination virtually if new; after a pass or a destination already virtually blue, add any virtually free vertex. If none exists, the virtual board has ended after Maker's move, and the winning property of S forces an edge already contained in the virtual—and therefore actual—Maker set. Thus every S-prescribed vertex is actually free. If no earlier win occurs, S's t-th move at x completes a k-edge e whose other k−1 vertices are among Maker's t−1 tokens. For t>k, exactly t−k≥1 tokens lie outside e, so moving one of them to x fills e. For t=k, k fresh tokens execute S and the lower bound gives equality. The exact state-space checker also verified this implication on every tested finite instance, including a 4-uniform n=9 instance with t=5>k.
claims.search_method: Independent invariant proof from the source definitions, followed by exact minimax and finite reachability-game enumeration explicitly including passes, relocations, and Breaker-winning cycles.

claims.claim: Uniform strict half-bound: every finite-theta k-uniform hypergraph H on n vertices satisfies θ(H)≤max{k,⌊(n−1)/2⌋}. In particular, if n≥2k+1 then θ(H)≤⌈n/2⌉−1.
claims.evidence: Finite θ implies that Maker wins the classical unlimited-token game, hence τ is finite. Classical play exhausts an n-vertex board after at most ⌈n/2⌉ Maker moves, so τ≤⌈n/2⌉. Claim 0 yields θ≤max{k,τ−1}≤max{k,⌈n/2⌉−1}=max{k,⌊(n−1)/2⌋}. When n≥2k+1, ⌈n/2⌉−1≥k, so the maximum is exactly ⌈n/2⌉−1. Integer identities and all enumerated finite game instances passed exact checks.
claims.search_method: Deduction from the independently verified compression lemma and the classical board-exhaustion bound, plus exact integer-identity and finite-game checks.

claims.claim: Exact order obstruction: a finite k-uniform hypergraph can attain θ(H)=⌈n/2⌉ only when n∈{2k−1,2k}; both orders are attainable.
claims.evidence: Write h=⌈n/2⌉. If h>k, Claim 1 gives θ≤h−1; if h<k, the simultaneous-token lower bound gives θ≥k>h. Hence equality θ=h forces h=k, equivalent for positive integers to n∈{2k−1,2k}. Conversely, on either order take the complete k-uniform hypergraph. Fewer than k tokens cannot fill an edge. Before Maker's k-th turn at most 2k−2 vertices have been occupied, so at least one vertex remains free; passes and relocations cannot increase that count. Maker therefore places k fresh tokens, which form an edge, proving θ=k=h. The checker solved these complete games with full token-game semantics for k=1,2,3,4.
claims.witness: For every positive k, the complete k-uniform hypergraphs on 2k−1 and 2k vertices attain θ(H)=k=⌈n/2⌉.
claims.search_method: Case split using the strict bound and k-token lower bound, constructive verification of both orders, and exact reachability-game checks of boundary examples.

target_evidence: The exact target asks whether some fixed k≥4 has arbitrarily large equality examples, or alternatively for a uniform stricter bound. The verified bound θ(H)≤max{k,⌊(n−1)/2⌋} is strictly below ⌈n/2⌉ whenever n≥2k+1, and the verified classification confines equality to n=2k−1 or n=2k. Thus each fixed k has only two possible equality orders, while complete k-uniform hypergraphs show those unavoidable exceptions are real. This settles the entire requested dichotomy at stronger, exact-order resolution. The draft's claimed_resolution of FULL is therefore ACCURATE.
